title: Line four is still holding
chapters: 00:00 Cold open: a caller who would not hang up|04:10 The room at 3 a.m.|15:45 Reading a voice|28:20 The calls you keep|39:05 Handing over at seven
pull: You learn to hear a kitchen. You can hear if there is a kettle on. You can hear if there are kids in the next room.
summary: Marcus Tull has taken emergency calls on the overnight shift for eleven years. He talks about the quiet hour, the busy hour, and what he listens for behind a caller's voice.
notes:
Marcus works twelve-hour nights, four on and four off, at a console with five screens and a foot pedal for the radio.

We recorded at the end of his last shift of the week, in the break room, with the door open so he could hear the floor.
transcript:
Mara: What is the first thing you hear when you pick up?

Marcus: The room. Before anybody says a word you get the room. Traffic, a television, wind. It tells you where to start.

title: The bridge goes up at midnight
chapters: 00:00 The horn|03:30 Eight minutes of nobody crossing|12:15 Barges, yachts and one swan|22:40 The log book since 1931|33:10 Swinging it shut
pull: Every car that waits for me thinks I am the slowest person in the city. Every boat thinks I am the fastest.
summary: Petra Lindqvist opens the Ash Canal swing bridge for boats from six in the evening until two in the morning. She keeps a paper log that goes back to 1931.
notes:
The bridge house has one chair, a kettle, a VHF radio and a ledger the size of a paving slab. Petra lets us read the entries from the winter of 1963.

Sound in this episode was recorded on the bridge deck; the creak at 22:40 is the bridge, not the microphone.
transcript: Petra: The rule is you never swing it with someone walking on it. Sounds obvious. You would be surprised.

title: Rooms 101 to 418, and the till
chapters: 00:00 Midnight close|06:20 Balancing the day|17:00 Guests who come down at 3|29:30 The fire panel|38:50 Breakfast staff arrive
pull: At three in the morning I am the accountant, the receptionist and the only person who knows where the spare key to the roof is.
summary: Soledad Fuentes closes the books on the hotel's day after midnight, then runs the front desk alone until the breakfast staff arrive.
notes:
The night audit at a 140-room hotel takes about two hours if nothing goes wrong. Soledad explains what goes wrong.

She asked us not to name the guests in the stories she tells, and we have not.
transcript: Soledad: The day is not over until the numbers say it is over. Sometimes that is one in the morning. Sometimes it is four.

title: Route 12 before the buses
chapters: 00:00 Salt yard at 10 p.m.|05:40 The route card|14:20 Hills in order of trouble|26:00 A car in the drift|35:30 Back to the yard
pull: My job is to make it look like nothing happened. If you wake up and the road is black, I did it right.
summary: Hal Brekke drives the plow on Route 12, the hill route, from ten at night until the first buses leave the depot at six.
notes:
Route 12 is 31 miles of the steepest streets in Corran. Hal has driven it for nine winters and knows each hill by the order it ices.

We rode the full route in the cab. The audio is loud in places; that is the blade.
transcript: Hal: Cobbler Hill first, always. If Cobbler Hill goes, the whole north side goes.

title: Calls after midnight
chapters: 00:00 Top of the hour|07:15 Who calls at 2 a.m.|19:40 The regulars|33:10 When a caller is not okay|46:00 Handing the mic to the morning show
pull: Most people who call at two in the morning do not want advice. They want somebody to know they are awake.
summary: Wren Abiodun hosts the midnight-to-five call-in show on CRN 94.1. She talks about the regular callers, the quiet ones, and the night a truck driver sang.
notes:
Wren has hosted the overnight show for six years. Her producer screens calls from a desk eleven feet away and they communicate mostly by sticky note.

Music in this episode is used with permission of CRN 94.1 (fictional).
transcript: Wren: I have a caller, Desmond, who rings every Tuesday at ten past two. If he does not ring, I worry.

title: The fish market opens at two
chapters: 00:00 Ice|04:50 The boats come in|13:30 Porters, buyers and the bell|24:10 Prices on a chalkboard|33:00 Hosing down at ten
pull: By six it is over. By six the restaurants have their fish and I have had my breakfast.
summary: Colm Hardesty has carried fish boxes at Saltgate since he was seventeen. The market opens at two, the bell goes at four, and by ten the floor is hosed down.
notes:
Saltgate is one of the last fish markets in the country that still sells by open outcry. Colm explains the bell, the chalkboard and the hand signals.

The episode includes the full four o'clock bell, unedited.
transcript: Colm: You can tell a good buyer from the way they look at the eyes. Not their eyes. The fish's eyes.

title: Ward 7B, seven to seven
chapters: 00:00 Handover at seven|06:30 The 2 a.m. round|18:10 Families in the corridor|30:45 What you eat at 4 a.m.|40:20 Handover again
pull: Night is when people tell you the truth. In the day they are brave for their visitors.
summary: Agnes Petrov has worked nights on a surgical ward for fourteen years. She talks about the 2 a.m. round, the families, and what keeps a night team together.
notes:
Agnes asked that no patients be described in a way that could identify them. Every story in this episode is told with details changed.

Recorded in the staff room after her shift, with permission from the hospital (fictional).
transcript: Agnes: The handover is the most important twenty minutes of the night. Everything I know has to go into somebody else's head.

title: Track gang, tunnel 3
chapters: 00:00 Last train|05:10 Juice off|14:50 Four hours in a tunnel|27:30 What lives down there|36:40 Juice on, everybody out
pull: We have four hours between the last train and the first train. Every minute is already spoken for.
summary: Rafe Ilunga leads a track gang that works the Eastern line after the last train. Four hours, no daylight, and a rail that has to be right by five.
notes:
The power to the third rail goes off at 0:50 and comes back at 4:45. Rafe's gang replaced eleven meters of rail the night we recorded.

Recorded with a hand recorder in tunnel 3, with a safety escort from the operator (fictional).
transcript: Rafe: You count people in, you count people out. If the numbers do not match, nobody goes home.

title: The bread comes out at four
chapters: 00:00 The alarm at midnight|03:45 Starter, flour, water|14:30 The oven at 3 a.m.|25:10 The first customer is a taxi driver|35:00 Sleep at ten
pull: The bread does not care that it is the middle of the night. It is ready when it is ready.
summary: Dellah Morrow has run the bakery on Corran Street for twenty years. She starts at one, pulls the first loaves at four, and opens the door at seven.
notes:
Morrow's bakes 340 loaves a night in a deck oven built in 1978. Dellah and two bakers do it in eight hours.

The first episode of season two and the cover story of Issue 9.
transcript: Dellah: People think bakers are morning people. We are not morning people. We are night people who get up very early.

title: Season two: the people up all night
pull: Eight nights, eight jobs, one city.
summary: A three-minute trailer for season two: bakers, porters, nurses, plow drivers and the people who keep a city running while it sleeps.

title: The milk round
chapters: 00:00 The float|06:00 340 doorsteps|17:20 Notes in empty bottles|27:00 Dogs|31:40 Back at the depot
pull: People leave me notes. Thirty years of notes. I have kept every one that made me laugh.
summary: Ted Ayre drives one of the last electric milk floats in Corran. He has delivered to the same 340 doorsteps since 1996.
notes: Ted's round covers four streets in Hollowmere. We walked the whole thing with him in the dark.
transcript: Ted: The quiet is the best part. Then the birds start, and that is the second best part.

title: Fares from the station rank
chapters: 00:00 The rank at 8 p.m.|08:10 The 11:40 from the capital|19:30 What people say in the back|30:00 Going home at 4
pull: The back seat is the only confessional left in the city.
summary: Amira Saleh drives a cab from Corran Central station from eight until four. She knows the train times better than the timetable.
notes: Amira has driven nights for nine years and has never had a shift without a story.
transcript: Amira: I know the last train is late before the board does.

title: Hot metal and the late edition
chapters: 00:00 Plates|09:20 The press starts|21:00 A late change at 1 a.m.|33:30 Bundles on the trucks
pull: When the press runs, you feel it in your feet before you hear it.
summary: Bernard Okoye has run the press at the Herald's print works for twenty-six years. The paper goes to bed at eleven; the press runs until three.
notes: The Herald prints 41,000 copies a night. Bernard is one of six people who make that happen.
transcript: Bernard: The late change is the best feeling in the job. Stop the press, swap the plate, go again.

title: Unedited: the four o'clock bell, all of it
chapters: 00:00 Ten to four|04:00 The bell|09:30 The first lot|18:20 Colm walks us out
pull: That bell is older than me, and I am old.
summary: Twenty-six minutes of raw tape from the Saltgate market floor, from ten to four until the first lots are sold. For members.
transcript: [Market floor sound. The bell rings at 04:00.]

title: Dellah and the sourdough argument
chapters: 00:00 Starter at 2 a.m.|06:40 The argument|14:30 Who won
pull: It is not an argument. I am right, and Joe is learning.
summary: The part we cut from episode 14: Dellah and her second baker disagree, loudly and at length, about hydration. For members.
notes: Recorded at 2:10 a.m. at the bench. Bonus episodes go to members first and stay in the back room.
